1. Identification Strategy
- Core design: Staggered difference-in-differences with event-study dynamics using modern estimators (Sun-Abraham or Callaway-Sant’Anna) on a developing-country panel, 1980–2004.
- Two complementary treatments to isolate “departures from neutrality” in ways the data can support:
  1) Hard non-neutrality: a sustained increase in tariff dispersion (standard deviation across tariff lines), holding average protection constant. This captures selective/targeted protection that distorts relative prices across activities.
  2) Broad liberalization (move toward neutrality): large, front-loaded reductions in average statutory tariffs.
- Outcomes: annual productivity growth (e.g., GDP per worker or TFP growth from PWT 6.1), and markers of structural transformation (where available in the file, e.g., manufacturing value added share; otherwise secondary outcome: investment rate or labor productivity growth in manufacturing if present).
- Why this works here:
  - Policy changes are staggered across countries and sizable (documented collapses in average tariffs and shifts in dispersion).
  - Country and year fixed effects absorb time-invariant differences and common global shocks; dynamics allow pre-trend testing and post-reform trajectories.
  - Focusing on dispersion separately from average tariffs speaks to “hard” selective interventions vs neutrality.

2. Treatment and Control
- Sample: Developing countries only for baseline estimations. High-income countries used only for placebo checks.
- Treatment A (Hard non-neutrality):
  - Treated unit-year: The first year t0 in which a country’s tariff dispersion rises above a high threshold and stays elevated, indicating a shift toward selective protection.
  - Operationalization:
    - Compute tariff dispersion percentile within the developing-country distribution by year. Define “high dispersion” as at/above the 75th percentile of the pooled distribution (robustness: 70th/80th).
    - Define an adoption year t0 as the first year a country enters and remains in high dispersion for at least 3 consecutive years.
  - Control: Countries not yet treated in a given year and never-treated countries (if any). Also include average tariff level as a covariate to isolate dispersion from overall protection.
- Treatment B (Move toward neutrality via liberalization):
  - Treated unit-year: The first year t0 in which a country initiates a large average tariff reduction.
  - Operationalization:
    - Identify “big liberalization” as a drop in the average statutory tariff of at least 30 percentage points within any 5-year window, with the event date set to the first year of that episode. Robustness: 20 p.p. in 3 years; or a fall into/below the 25th percentile of the country-specific historical distribution sustained for 3 years.
  - Control: Not-yet-treated and never-treated countries.
- Event time: Estimate dynamic effects k = −10,…,+10 years around t0 (where data allow), excluding k = −1 as the baseline lead.
- Running variable and cutoff: Not applicable (not RDD).

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Parallel trends (conditional): In the absence of treatment, treated and control countries would have exhibited similar outcome trends conditional on country FE, year FE, and covariates (e.g., average tariff when studying dispersion; exchange-rate movements).
  - Plausibility: Many reforms were driven by global waves and conditionality, but there is heterogeneity in timing and intensity. Pre-trend tests in event studies help evaluate plausibility.
- No anticipatory outcome movements: Outcomes do not change in anticipation before treatment beyond smooth trends.
  - Plausibility: Medium. Reforms are sometimes announced ahead of time; we will look for anticipatory deviations in the leads and, if detected, redefine t0 (e.g., to announcement) or trim early leads.
- No time-varying confounders perfectly aligned with treatment that are not controlled for: Major concurrent reforms (privatization, macro stabilization, exchange-rate regime switches) could confound effects.
  - Plausibility: Mixed. We will partial out proxies (exchange-rate changes, inflation if available, global commodity-price-year FE via region×year FE) and conduct exclusion windows around IMF programs (if flagged in the data; otherwise sensitivity excluding known crisis years).
- SUTVA/no interference: A country’s treatment does not directly affect outcomes in control countries.
  - Plausibility: Partial. Trade is networked. We will test robustness by excluding large neighbors/trade hubs, and by using region-year FE to absorb regional contagion.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
- Endogenous policy timing (reverse causality): Countries may raise dispersion in response to weak productivity or falling sectors; liberalize after crises. This biases estimates.
  - Mitigation:
    - Event-study pre-trends and placebo tests; drop countries with strong negative pre-trends.
    - Include country-specific linear trends.
    - Control for macro conditions (Δlog nominal exchange rate, inflation if available).
    - Sensitivity excluding early reformers or crisis-driven reforms; alternative treatment thresholds.
- Concurrent reforms/programs: IMF stabilization, privatizations, VAT adoption may coincide with tariff reforms.
  - Mitigation:
    - Region×year FE.
    - Explicit controls for fiscal pressure (tariff revenue/trade), attempting to separate optimal-tax motives from selective protection.
    - Exclusion windows around known adjustment episodes; re-estimate.
- Measurement error in tariff dispersion or statutory averages:
  - Mitigation:
    - Smooth variables with 3-year moving averages when defining treatment, but estimate on annual outcomes.
    - Use tariff revenue/trade as an outcome-free proxy to verify if statutory shifts reflect de facto changes; re-define treatment using both statutory and revenue-based thresholds as robustness.

5. R Code Outline
Assumptions:
- A CSV country_panel.csv contains: country, iso3c, year, dev (1=developing), avg_tariff, tariff_sd, tariff_rev_share, trade_share_real_pwt, trade_share_nominal, exrate_nominal, fdi_gdp, rgdpw (real GDP per worker, PWT 6.1) or alternatively gdp_pc; optional manuf_share.
- We focus on 1980–2004 and dev==1.

R code:

```r
# Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)       # feols + sunab for staggered DID
library(data.table)

# 1) Load data
df <- fread("country_panel.csv") %>%
  mutate(year = as.integer(year)) %>%
  filter(year >= 1980, year <= 2004, dev == 1)

# 2) Construct outcomes
# Primary outcome: GDP per worker growth (log difference)
df <- df %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    y = 100 * (log(rgdpw) - lag(log(rgdpw))),  # % growth
    d_exrate = 100 * (log(exrate_nominal) - lag(log(exrate_nominal)))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# 3) Define Treatment A: Hard non-neutrality via tariff dispersion
# Compute pooled 75th percentile threshold (within developing countries, all years)
p75_disp <- quantile(df$tariff_sd, probs = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)

df <- df %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    high_disp = as.integer(tariff_sd >= p75_disp),
    # 3-year sustained indicator to avoid transients
    high_disp_roll3 = zoo::rollapplyr(high_disp, width = 3, partial = FALSE, align = "left", FUN = function(x) as.integer(all(x == 1))),
    # adoption year = first year where high_disp persists for >=3 years
    adopt_year_hard = ifelse(high_disp == 1 & high_disp_roll3 == 1 & is.na(lag(high_disp, 1, default = 0)), year, NA_integer_)
  ) %>%
  mutate(adopt_year_hard = min(adopt_year_hard, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%  # first such year
  mutate(adopt_year_hard = ifelse(is.infinite(adopt_year_hard), NA_integer_, adopt_year_hard)) %>%
  ungroup()

# 4) Define Treatment B: Big liberalization (avg tariff falls >=30 p.p. over 5 years)
df <- df %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    avg_tariff_lead5 = dplyr::lead(avg_tariff, 5),
    big_lib = as.integer(!is.na(avg_tariff_lead5) & (avg_tariff - avg_tariff_lead5) >= 30),
    adopt_year_lib = ifelse(big_lib == 1 & is.na(lag(big_lib, 1, default = 0)), year, NA_integer_)
  ) %>%
  mutate(adopt_year_lib = min(adopt_year_lib, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(adopt_year_lib = ifelse(is.infinite(adopt_year_lib), NA_integer_, adopt_year_lib)) %>%
  ungroup()

# 5) Clean analysis sample: need outcome and controls
df_est <- df %>%
  filter(!is.na(y), !is.na(avg_tariff), !is.na(tariff_sd)) %>%
  mutate(t = year - 1980)  # for country-specific trends if used

# 6) Event-study: Treatment A (hard non-neutrality via dispersion)
# Controls: avg_tariff, d_exrate, tariff_rev_share (proxy fiscal pressure) if available
est_hard <- feols(
  y ~ sunab(adopt_year_hard, year, ref.p = -1) + avg_tariff + d_exrate + tariff_rev_share |
    country + year,
  cluster = ~ country,
  data = df_est
)

summary(est_hard)
iplot(est_hard, ref.line = 0, main = "Event study: Increase in tariff dispersion")

# 7) Event-study: Treatment B (big liberalization)
# Controls: tariff_sd, d_exrate, tariff_rev_share
est_lib <- feols(
  y ~ sunab(adopt_year_lib, year, ref.p = -1) + tariff_sd + d_exrate + tariff_rev_share |
    country + year,
  cluster = ~ country,
  data = df_est
)

summary(est_lib)
iplot(est_lib, ref.line = 0, main = "Event study: Large average tariff cut")

# 8) Robustness A: Alternative thresholds
# Hard non-neutrality with 80th percentile
p80_disp <- quantile(df$tariff_sd, probs = 0.80, na.rm = TRUE)
df_alt <- df %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    high_disp80 = as.integer(tariff_sd >= p80_disp),
    high_disp80_roll3 = zoo::rollapplyr(high_disp80, 3, partial = FALSE, align = "left",
                                        FUN = function(x) as.integer(all(x == 1))),
    adopt_year_hard80 = ifelse(high_disp80 == 1 & high_disp80_roll3 == 1 & is.na(lag(high_disp80, 1, default = 0)), year, NA_integer_)
  ) %>%
  mutate(adopt_year_hard80 = min(adopt_year_hard80, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(adopt_year_hard80 = ifelse(is.infinite(adopt_year_hard80), NA_integer_, adopt_year_hard80)) %>%
  ungroup()

est_hard80 <- feols(
  y ~ sunab(adopt_year_hard80, year, ref.p = -1) + avg_tariff + d_exrate + tariff_rev_share |
    country + year,
  cluster = ~ country,
  data = df_alt %>% filter(!is.na(y))
)

summary(est_hard80)

# 9) Robustness B: Country-specific linear trends
est_lib_trend <- feols(
  y ~ sunab(adopt_year_lib, year, ref.p = -1) + tariff_sd + d_exrate + tariff_rev_share + i(country, t) |
    country + year,
  cluster = ~ country,
  data = df_est
)

summary(est_lib_trend)
```

Notes:
- sunab handles heterogeneous treatment timing properly under TWFE.
- If the file includes TFP growth or manufacturing share, define y accordingly and re-run. If using levels (e.g., manufacturing share), include lagged DV or focus on medium-run changes (e.g., 3-year forward differences).

6. Expected Results
- Hard non-neutrality (rising tariff dispersion):
  - Prior: Negative effect on aggregate productivity growth and structural transformation. Selective protection typically misallocates resources, raises input costs, and entrenches rents absent strong governance.
  - Magnitude: A 1 SD sustained increase in dispersion is expected to lower annual GDP per worker growth by roughly 0.2–0.4 percentage points over the subsequent 5–10 years.
- Broad liberalization (large average tariff cuts toward neutrality):
  - Prior: Positive medium-run effect on productivity growth through competitive pressure, imported inputs/technology; short-run effects may be muted if macro is unstable.
  - Magnitude: A 10 p.p. fall in average tariffs is expected to raise annual GDP per worker growth by ~0.2–0.5 percentage points in the medium run (so a 30 p.p. “big” cut yields ~0.6–1.5 p.p. higher growth over 3–7 years), with heterogeneity by initial distortions and macro stability.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (for staggered DID with event studies)
- C1: Parallel trends supported by pre-trend tests and controls (score: 0.7). We will explicitly test, but crises and selection remain concerns.
- C2: No anticipation (score: 0.6). Some anticipation likely; we will inspect leads and, if needed, re-date events or trim.
- C3: No important time-varying confounders unaccounted for (score: 0.6). We add macro controls and region-year FE proxies; residual confounding possible.
- C4: No interference/spillovers (score: 0.5). Trade linkages create potential spillovers; we will run leave-one-region-out checks.
- C5: Correct handling of staggered timing/heterogeneous effects (score: 1.0). We use Sun-Abraham event-study implementation and report cohort-specific dynamics.

Extensions if additional data can be added:
- Add explicit measures of “soft” coordination policies (export promotion agencies, supplier-development programs, SEZ rollouts) and FDI tax incentive adoptions (e.g., from UNCTAD or IMF fiscal incentives databases). Then estimate a three-way comparison: hard vs soft vs neutral.
- Bartik IV for average-tariff changes using global, sector-specific tariff schedules interacted with pre-reform export structure (if sectoral trade/composition data can be merged), to further mitigate endogeneity of tariff reforms.
